modules.title: Thyroid Disorders, Short Stature and Skeletal Dysplasias

lessonTopics.title: Congenital Hypothyroidism: Newborn Screening, Levothyroxine Timing and Etiologies

mustKnow.fact: Newborn dried blood spot screening for TSH must be performed between 48 and 72 hours of life to avoid false-positive recall from the physiological neonatal TSH surge that peaks at 30 minutes after birth.

Thyroid dysgenesis (ectopia 60%, athyreosis 25%, hypoplasia 5%) accounts for 85% of permanent congenital hypothyroidism, while thyroid dyshormonogenesis (autosomal recessive defects in TPO, TG, DUOX2, SLC5A5) accounts for 15%.
Oral levothyroxine must be initiated within the first two weeks of life at 10-15 mcg/kg/day to rapidly normalize serum free T4 within 3-7 days and TSH within 2-4 weeks, preserving IQ.

mustKnow.term: Soy and iron interference with absorption
mustKnow.fact: Levothyroxine tablets should be crushed in breast milk or water; co-administration with soy formulas, calcium carbonate, iron supplements, and aluminum hydroxide inhibits intestinal absorption and causes persistent TSH elevation.

mustKnow.term: Target serum free T4 monitoring range
mustKnow.fact: During the first year of life, serum free T4 should be maintained in the upper half of the age-specific reference range (1.4-2.3 ng/dL) with TSH normalized between 0.5 and 2.0 mIU/L.

Transient hypothyroidism is caused by maternal TSH receptor blocking antibodies (TRBAb), maternal antithyroid drug ingestion, iodine deficiency, or excess topical iodinated antiseptic exposure in neonates.

mustKnow.term: Trial off levothyroxine at age 3 years
mustKnow.fact: In children without documented thyroid ectopia or aplasia on infant imaging, a trial off levothyroxine for 4-6 weeks at age 3 years assesses whether hypothyroidism is permanent or transient.

Pendred syndrome is an autosomal recessive mutation in SLC26A4 encoding pendrin, pairing congenital dyshormonogenic goitrous hypothyroidism with sensorineural hearing loss and enlarged vestibular aqueducts.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Autoimmune Thyroid Disease: Hashimoto, Graves and Antithyroid Therapies

mustKnow.fact: Hashimoto (chronic lymphocytic) thyroiditis is the leading cause of acquired hypothyroidism and goiter in children, diagnosed by elevated serum anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) in > 90% and anti-thyroglobulin (anti-TG) antibodies.

Initial presentation of Hashimoto thyroiditis can feature transient mild hyperthyroidism (hashitoxicosis) due to inflammatory disruption of thyroid follicles, which spontaneously subsides in weeks to months without antithyroid drugs.

Pediatric Graves disease is driven by autoantibodies that bind and stimulate the TSH receptor (TRAb / TSI), causing smooth diffuse vascular goiter, weight loss, heat intolerance, proptosis, and accelerated linear growth.

Oral methimazole (0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day once daily, max 30 mg) is the sole recommended first-line antithyroid drug in children; propylthiouracil (PTU) is strictly black-box contraindicated due to fatal fulminant hepatic necrosis.

Parents must be educated to stop methimazole immediately and obtain urgent absolute neutrophil count (ANC) if the child develops fever, sore throat, or mouth ulceration; agranulocytosis (ANC < 500/mm³) occurs in 0.3-0.5%.
Propranolol (1-2 mg/kg/day divided TID) or atenolol provides immediate symptomatic relief of palpitations, tachycardia, and severe tremor until methimazole achieves euthyroid state at 4-8 weeks.

mustKnow.term: Definitive Graves therapies (Radioactive iodine vs Surgery)
mustKnow.fact: If medical remission is not achieved after 2-3 years of methimazole, definitive treatment options are total thyroidectomy or 131-I radioiodine ablation (doses > 150-200 microCi/g, preferably in children > 5-10 years).

Transplacental passage of maternal TRAb causes transient neonatal thyrotoxicosis (fetal tachycardia, craniosynostosis, cardiac failure), treated with methimazole, Lugol iodine, and propranolol, resolving by 3-4 months as maternal IgG clears.

lessonTopics.title: Short Stature and Growth Failure: GHD Auxology, Provocative Tests and Pituitary MRI

mustKnow.fact: Short stature is defined as height > 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex (height SDS < -2.0, or < 3rd percentile); growth failure is annual height velocity < 25th percentile for age over 6-12 months.
Target height calculation: For boys = [Father height + Mother height + 13 cm] / 2; For girls = [Father height - 13 cm + Mother height] / 2; target range is ± 8.5 cm (± 2 SD).
Serum IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 reflect integrated GH secretion; levels < -2 SD for age and pubertal stage support GH deficiency or GH insensitivity, unaffected by pulsatility.
Definitive diagnosis of GHD requires failure to reach peak GH >= 7-10 ng/mL on two separate provocative stimulation tests (clonidine, arginine, glucagon, or insulin tolerance test).

Pre-pubertal boys > 10 years and girls > 9 years with delayed bone age require sex-steroid priming (intramuscular testosterone or oral estradiol) prior to GH testing to prevent false-positive subnormal peaks.

mustKnow.term: Pituitary MRI findings in congenital GHD
mustKnow.fact: Brain MRI evaluates the hypothalamic-pituitary axis; the triad of pituitary stalk interruption syndrome consists of ectopic posterior pituitary bright spot, hypoplastic/absent infundibulum, and anterior pituitary hypoplasia.
Somatropin is initiated at 0.16-0.24 mg/kg/week (divided into daily subcutaneous bedtime injections), monitoring linear growth and titrating dose to maintain serum IGF-1 between 0 and +2 SDS.

Children on GH must be monitored for slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE, limping or knee pain), idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri, headache/vomiting), scoliosis progression, and hyperglycemia.

lessonTopics.title: Turner Syndrome 45,X: Auxology, High-Dose rhGH, Pubertal Induction and Aortic Surveillance

mustKnow.fact: Turner syndrome affects 1 in 2000 liveborn females; 45,X monosomy accounts for 45-50%, while mosaicism (45,X/46,XX), isochromosome Xq [46,X,i(Xq)], and ring X chromosomes make up the remainder.
mustKnow.source: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Turner Syndrome

mustKnow.fact: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for SRY / Y-chromosome material is mandatory in all Turner patients; presence of cryptic Y material carries a 15-30% risk of gonadoblastoma, requiring prophylactic bilateral gonadectomy.

mustKnow.term: SHOX gene haploinsufficiency and rhGH dosing
mustKnow.fact: Short stature is caused by haploinsufficiency of the SHOX gene in the pseudoautosomal region (PAR1); rhGH is started early (around age 4-6) at higher doses (0.35-0.375 mg/kg/week) to achieve adult height gain of 5-8 cm.

Pubertal induction begins around age 11-12 years using transdermal 17-beta estradiol at low initial doses (1/8 to 1/4 adult dose, 3-6 mcg/day patch) with gradual escalation over 2-3 years to mimic normal physiology and maximize uterine growth.

Oral micronized progesterone (100-200 mg daily for 10-12 days per month) is added only after 2 years of estrogen therapy or when breakthrough vaginal bleeding occurs, ensuring complete breast ductal development.

Bicuspid aortic valve (30%) and coarctation of the aorta (12%) are prevalent; aortic size index (ASI = aortic root diameter / BSA) > 2.0 cm/m² or aortic root Z-score > 2.5 identifies high risk for fatal aortic dissection.
Renal ultrasonography is recommended at diagnosis to screen for congenital anomalies (found in 30-40%), most commonly horseshoe kidney (pelvic fusion) and duplicated collecting system.
Girls with Turner syndrome have high prevalence of Hashimoto thyroiditis (30%) and celiac disease (5-8%), mandating annual thyroid function tests and baseline celiac serology (anti-tTG IgA).

lessonTopics.title: Constitutional Delay vs Familial Short Stature: Bone Age Delay and Testosterone Priming

mustKnow.term: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) triad
mustKnow.fact: CDGP is characterized by delayed bone age (> 2 years behind chronological age), normal height velocity (>= 4-5 cm/year), delayed pubertal onset, and positive family history of late puberty (late bloomer), reaching normal adult height.

In familial short stature, bone age is concordant with chronological age (no delay), linear growth velocity is normal, pubertal timing is normal, and projected adult height falls exactly within mid-parental target range.
Bone age is evaluated via single left hand-wrist radiograph using the Greulich and Pyle atlas or Tanner-Whitehouse (TW3) method; delay > 2 standard deviations signifies skeletal maturation delay.

In adolescent boys >= 14 years with CDGP experiencing psychological distress, low-dose testosterone enanthate (50-100 mg IM monthly for 3-6 months) safely accelerates growth velocity and jump-starts hypothalamic GnRH without compromising final adult height.

In adolescent girls >= 13 years with CDGP, low-dose oral ethinyl estradiol (2-5 mcg daily) or transdermal estradiol for 3-6 months promotes secondary sexual characteristics and accelerates linear growth velocity.
The Bayley-Pinneau tables predict final adult height based on current height and Greulich-Pyle bone age, distinguishing benign CDGP from true pathological growth hormone deficiency.

Red flags signaling pathological growth failure include height crossing percentiles downward, subnormal height velocity (< 4 cm/year), disproportionate limb-to-trunk ratio (skeletal dysplasias), and dysmorphic features.
Children born Small for Gestational Age (SGA: birth weight or length < -2 SD) who fail to show spontaneous catch-up growth by 2-4 years of age qualify for rhGH therapy (0.067 mg/kg/day).

modules.title: Adrenal Cortex, CAH and Differences of Sex Development

lessonTopics.title: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia: 21-Hydroxylase Deficiency, 17-OHP and Crisis Care

mustKnow.fact: Deficiency of 21-hydroxylase (CYP21A2 gene on chromosome 6p21.3) accounts for > 90-95% of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, resulting in impaired cortisol and aldosterone synthesis with precursor shunting into androgens.
Classic CAH is divided into salt-wasting (75%, severe aldosterone deficiency, neonatal shock) and simple virilizing (25%, adequate aldosterone, prenatal virilization in females).
Salt-wasting neonates present at 7-14 days of life with vomiting, weight loss, lethargy, hyponatremia (Na < 125 mEq/L), hyperkalemia (K > 7.0 mEq/L), metabolic acidosis, and hypovolemic shock.
Newborn blood spot screening measures 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) via immunoassay or tandem mass spectrometry; levels > 30-100 nmol/L confirm classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

Immediate resuscitation requires an IV bolus of 0.9% normal saline (20 mL/kg) with 5-10% dextrose to treat hypovolemia and hypoglycemia, followed by parenteral hydrocortisone; potassium-containing fluids are strictly forbidden.
Maintenance therapy requires oral hydrocortisone (10-15 mg/m²/day divided TID) and fludrocortisone (0.05-0.2 mg/day) plus oral sodium chloride supplements (1-2 g/day, 17-34 mEq/day) in infants.

Maternal dexamethasone (20 mcg/kg/day) initiated before 9 weeks gestation suppresses fetal ACTH and virilization in at-risk female fetuses; requires early non-invasive prenatal sex determination via cell-free fetal DNA.

Males with poorly controlled CAH develop bilateral testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART) stimulated by chronic ACTH elevation, causing testicular discomfort and infertility, detected by routine testicular ultrasound.

lessonTopics.title: Non-Classic CAH, 11-Beta and 17-Alpha Hydroxylase Deficiencies: Blood Pressure Signatures

mustKnow.fact: NCCAH is an autosomal recessive condition affecting 1 in 200 to 1 in 1000 individuals (higher in Ashkenazi Jews), caused by mild CYP21A2 missense variants (e.g., p.Val281Leu) retaining 20-50% enzyme activity.
Diagnosis of NCCAH is established by a 60-minute cosyntropin (ACTH 250 mcg) stimulation test yielding stimulated 17-OHP > 30 nmol/L (> 1000 ng/dL); basal levels may be normal or mildly elevated.

Deficiency of CYP11B1 (5-8% of CAH) causes accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC, a potent mineralocorticoid) and 11-deoxycortisol, producing severe low-renin hypertension and hypokalemia alongside female virilization.

CYP17A1 deficiency blocks both cortisol and sex steroid production, causing massive mineralocorticoid excess (hypertension, hypokalemia) combined with sexual infantilism in 46,XX and female external genitalia in 46,XY.

HSD3B2 deficiency impairs all three steroid pathways, producing severe salt wasting, elevated DHEA-to-androstenedione ratio, ambiguous genitalia in 46,XY (undervirilization) and mild virilization in 46,XX.

Mutations in steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (StAR) prevent cholesterol entry into mitochondria, producing complete absence of all steroids, fatal neonatal salt-wasting, and female phenotype in all genetic sexes.

POR deficiency impairs multiple microsomal enzymes (CYP21A2, CYP17A1, CYP51A1), causing disordered steroidogenesis alongside skeletal craniosynostosis (Antley-Bixler syndrome) and maternal virilization during pregnancy.

Both 21-OH and 11-OH deficiencies virilize female fetuses; the critical differentiator is blood pressure and renin: 21-OH features hypotension, salt loss, and high renin, whereas 11-OH features hypertension and suppressed renin.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Adrenal Crisis and Addison Disease: Stress Dosing and Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndromes

mustKnow.fact: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) in children is mostly autoimmune (85%), confirmed by positive anti-21-hydroxylase autoantibodies, or due to X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1) in boys.

Loss of cortisol negative feedback induces massive pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) and ACTH hypersecretion, whose alpha-MSH subunit stimulates melanocytes, creating classic hyperpigmentation of palmar creases, gingiva, and scars.

Adrenal crisis is precipitated by physiological stress (gastroenteritis, high fever, surgery) in cortisol-deficient children, characterized by refractory hypotension, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia.

In acute adrenal crisis, intramuscular or intravenous hydrocortisone is administered immediately: 25 mg for infants (< 1 year), 50 mg for children (1-5 years), and 100 mg for older children (> 5 years).
During febrile illness (> 38.5°C) or significant physical trauma, oral maintenance hydrocortisone must be doubled or tripled (30-50 mg/m²/day) divided into 3-4 doses until clinical recovery.

APS-1 is an autosomal recessive mutation in the AIRE gene (21q22.3), defined by >= 2 of triad: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (infancy), hypoparathyroidism (childhood), and Addison disease (adolescence).
APS-2 is polygenic (HLA-DR3/DR4 association), defined by Addison disease accompanied by autoimmune thyroid disease (Schmidt syndrome) and/or Type 1 diabetes mellitus.

mustKnow.term: Emergency injectable hydrocortisone and medic-alert identification
mustKnow.fact: Every child with adrenal insufficiency must carry an emergency intramuscular hydrocortisone kit (Solu-Cortef Act-O-Vial 100 mg) and wear an indelible medical alert bracelet at all times.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Cushing Syndrome: Dexamethasone Testing, IPSS and Etiological Localization

mustKnow.term: Cushing syndrome clinical hallmark in children
mustKnow.fact: The single most specific clinical hallmark of pediatric Cushing syndrome is the combination of rapid progressive weight gain alongside arrest or deceleration of linear growth velocity (crossing height percentiles downward).

Iatrogenic (exogenous) administration of topical, inhaled, or systemic corticosteroids is by far the most common cause of Cushingoid features in children, accompanied by suppressed endogenous ACTH and cortisol.

Endogenous hypercortisolism is established by >= 2 abnormal screening tests: 24-hour urinary free cortisol (> 3x upper normal limit), midnight salivary cortisol (> 4 nmol/L), or 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test.

Morning plasma ACTH differentiates etiology: ACTH < 5 pg/mL indicates primary adrenal disease (adenoma, carcinoma, PPNAD), while ACTH > 15-20 pg/mL indicates ACTH-dependent Cushing disease or ectopic ACTH.

mustKnow.term: Cushing disease predominance in children > 7 years
mustKnow.fact: In children older than 7 years, ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) causes > 85% of endogenous hypercortisolemia; in infants < 1 year, functioning adrenal tumors dominate.

When pituitary MRI is normal or equivocal in ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism, BIPSS with CRH stimulation confirms pituitary source if the central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient is >= 2.0 basal or >= 3.0 post-CRH.

mustKnow.term: Carney complex and PPNAD PRKAR1A genetics
mustKnow.fact: Primary Pigmented Nodular Adrenocortical Disease (PPNAD) is caused by inactivating mutations in PRKAR1A (17q24.2), manifesting as paradoxical cortisol rise after dexamethasone (Liddle test) and cardiac myxomas.

Infants with McCune-Albright syndrome (mosaic GNAS mutation) can present with ACTH-independent bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia, which often spontaneously regresses as mutant clones exhaust.

lessonTopics.title: 46,XY Differences of Sex Development: Androgen Insensitivity, 5-ARD and Gonadectomy Timing

mustKnow.fact: 46,XY DSD results from impaired testis development (SRY/SOX9 gonadal dysgenesis), impaired androgen synthesis (CYP17A1, HSD17B3), or impaired androgen action (androgen receptor or 5-alpha-reductase-2 defects).

CAIS is an X-linked recessive androgen receptor (AR) mutation presenting with completely normal female external genitalia, blind-ending vagina, absent uterus/fallopian tubes (due to normal Sertoli anti-Müllerian hormone AMH), and bilateral intra-abdominal testes.

In CAIS, bilateral gonadectomy is safely deferred until late adolescence (after completion of spontaneous female puberty driven by aromatization of endogenous testicular androgens), with malignancy risk < 2-5% before age 20.

PAIS exhibits partial AR responsiveness, presenting with ambiguous genitalia (micropenis, bifid scrotum, perineoscrotal hypospadias) and gynecomastia at puberty; response to high-dose testosterone therapy is variable.

Autosomal recessive SRD5A2 mutations impair dihydrotestosterone (DHT) synthesis, causing ambiguous genitalia at birth but dramatic virilization at puberty (phallic growth, muscle mass, voice deepening) due to testosterone surge.
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) stimulation testing yields an abnormally elevated serum testosterone-to-DHT ratio (> 20-30:1) in 5-alpha-reductase deficiency compared to normal (< 10:1).

PMDS is caused by mutations in AMH or AMHR2, presenting in phenotypically normal 46,XY males who are found to have uterus and fallopian tubes during surgery for inguinal hernia (hernia uteri inguinalis) or cryptorchidism.
In 46,XY partial gonadal dysgenesis with intra-abdominal gonads, the risk of gonadoblastoma and seminoma exceeds 30-50%, mandating early prophylactic laparoscopic gonadectomy upon diagnosis.

lessonTopics.title: 46,XX Differences of Sex Development: Virilization, Ovotesticular DSD and Multidisciplinary Care

mustKnow.term: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia as dominant cause
mustKnow.fact: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (specifically 21-hydroxylase deficiency) accounts for > 90% of all 46,XX DSD cases, driven by excessive fetal adrenal androgen production virilizing external genitalia.

Prader classification grades 46,XX virilization: Stage I (mild clitoromegaly), Stage II (clitoromegaly with narrow urogenital sinus), Stage III (urogenital sinus with single perineal opening), Stage IV (phallic urethra), to Stage V (complete penile urethra with scrotal fusion).

Because the ovaries lack Sertoli cells and do not secrete anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), 46,XX DSD patients possess completely normal internal Müllerian structures: uterus, fallopian tubes, and upper vagina.

Placental aromatase deficiency fails to convert fetal DHEA-S to estrogens, causing severe maternal virilization during pregnancy (deepening voice, clitoromegaly) alongside ambiguous genitalia in 46,XX neonate.
Ovotesticular DSD requires histological confirmation of both ovarian follicles and testicular seminiferous tubules in the same individual (either separate ovary and testis, or combined ovotestis).
Over 60-70% of ovotesticular DSD patients have a 46,XX karyotype (frequently SRY-negative with cryptic SOX9 duplication), while 10% are 46,XY and the remainder are 46,XX/46,XY chimeras.

Modern consensus guidelines mandate that sex assignment and management be coordinated by a multidisciplinary team (pediatric endocrinologist, urologist, geneticist, psychologist, ethicist) before registering gender.
Current consensus emphasizes deferring non-urgent feminizing genitoplasty (clitoroplasty and vaginoplasty) until the individual is old enough to participate meaningfully in informed consent.

modules.title: Precocious and Delayed Puberty, Hypogonadism and Gynecomastia

lessonTopics.title: Central Precocious Puberty: Hypothalamic Hamartoma, GnRH Testing and Leuprolide

mustKnow.term: Chronological age cutoffs for precocious puberty
mustKnow.fact: Precocious puberty is defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years of age in girls (breast development, thelarche) and before 9 years of age in boys (testicular volume >= 4 mL).

Central precocious puberty (CPP) is gonadotropin-dependent, caused by premature maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis, maintaining normal pubertal sequence and concordant testicular enlargement in boys.
Over 80-90% of CPP cases in girls are idiopathic, whereas in boys > 50% are pathological, secondary to CNS lesions (hypothalamic hamartoma, astrocytoma, hydrocephalus, germinoma).
Hypothalamic hamartomas are non-neoplastic congenital heterotopias composed of GnRH-secreting neurons, presenting with CPP and pathognomonic refractory gelastic (laughing) seizures.

mustKnow.term: GnRH / Leuprolide stimulation test diagnostic peak
mustKnow.fact: Diagnosis is confirmed by GnRH stimulation test: a peak LH > 5.0 IU/L (or stimulated LH-to-FSH ratio > 0.66) indicates pubertal activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

First-line therapy is depot GnRH agonist (leuprolide acetate 7.5-11.25 mg IM monthly, or 30 mg every 3 months) to continuously saturate and desensitize pituitary GnRH receptors, halting LH/FSH secretion.

mustKnow.term: Treatment monitoring and adult height preservation
mustKnow.fact: Therapy halts bone age progression and prevents premature epiphyseal fusion, preserving final adult height; treatment is continued until chronological age 11 years in girls and 12 years in boys.
Familial central precocious puberty is most frequently caused by paternally inherited inactivating mutations in makorin ring finger protein 3 (MKRN3 on 15q11.2) or delta-like 1 (DLK1 on 14q32.2).

lessonTopics.title: Peripheral Precocious Puberty: McCune-Albright, Testotoxicosis and Aromatase Blockade

mustKnow.fact: Peripheral precocious puberty results from autonomous sex steroid production independent of pituitary LH/FSH; serum gonadotropins remain suppressed (LH < 0.1 IU/L) even after GnRH stimulation.

mustKnow.term: McCune-Albright syndrome triad and somatic GNAS
mustKnow.fact: McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by postzygotic somatic mosaic activating mutations in GNAS (p.Arg201), presenting with triad of peripheral precocious puberty (large ovarian cysts), café-au-lait spots (coast of Maine), and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia.
Young girls with McCune-Albright present with sudden painless vaginal bleeding from estrogen withdrawal as autonomous luteinized follicular cysts spontaneously form and regress.

mustKnow.term: Aromatase inhibitor and estrogen blocker therapy
mustKnow.fact: Medical therapy for McCune-Albright precocity utilizes third-generation aromatase inhibitors (letrozole 2.5 mg/day) combined with selective estrogen receptor modulators (tamoxifen) to arrest vaginal bleeding and skeletal maturation.

Testotoxicosis is an autosomal dominant condition caused by activating mutations in LHCGR (2p21), driving constitutive Leydig cell testosterone secretion in boys by age 2-4 years despite prepubertal LH.

Testotoxicosis is treated with an anti-androgen (bicalutamide or spironolactone) combined with an aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole or letrozole) to block androgen receptors and prevent estrogen-mediated epiphyseal closure.

Chronic exposure to high peripheral sex steroid levels accelerates hypothalamic maturation; upon medical suppression of peripheral steroids, a secondary true central precocious puberty commonly erupts, requiring GnRH agonists.

Ovarian juvenile granulosa cell tumors (producing estradiol and inhibin B) and testicular Leydig cell tumors (unilateral testicular mass, asymmetric enlargement) are surgical causes of peripheral precocity.

lessonTopics.title: Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism and Kallmann Syndrome: Olfactory and Neuroendocrine Axes

mustKnow.fact: Delayed puberty is absence of initial secondary sexual signs by 13 years in girls (no breast buds) or 14 years in boys (testicular volume < 4 mL), or absence of menarche by 15-16 years.
Characterized by inappropriately low or undetectable serum LH and FSH in the presence of subnormal sex steroids (testosterone < 20 ng/dL in boys, estradiol < 10 pg/mL in girls).

Kallmann syndrome pairs congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia or hyposmia due to defective embryonic co-migration of GnRH neuroendocrine cells and olfactory axons from the olfactory placode.
X-linked Kallmann is caused by ANOS1 / KAL1 mutations (Xp22.3, paired with bimanual synkinesia and unilateral renal agenesis); autosomal forms involve FGFR1, PROKR2, and CHD7.
Patients with nIHH have completely intact sense of smell, harboring mutations in GNRHR, TAC3 / TACR3 (neurokinin B pathway), KISS1 / KISS1R (kisspeptin pathway), or GNRH1.

mustKnow.term: Mini-puberty window for early infant diagnosis
mustKnow.fact: During the neonatal mini-puberty (1-6 months of life), normal infants exhibit transient activation of LH/FSH and testosterone/estradiol; absence of mini-puberty in an infant boy with cryptorchidism and micropenis identifies congenital hypogonadism.

mustKnow.term: Pubertal induction regimen in adolescent boys
mustKnow.fact: Pubertal induction begins with low-dose depot testosterone (testosterone enanthate 50 mg IM monthly for 6 months, escalating by 50 mg every 6 months to adult dose 200 mg every 2 weeks).

Unlike testosterone replacement which does not stimulate spermatogenesis, gonadotropin therapy combining hCG (LH analog, 1000-2000 IU twice weekly) with recombinant FSH induces testicular growth and fertile spermatogenesis.

lessonTopics.title: Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism: Klinefelter Syndrome 47,XXY, Dysgenesis and Hormone Replacement

mustKnow.fact: Characterized by primary gonadal failure with markedly elevated serum gonadotropins (FSH and LH > 20-40 IU/L) due to absence of negative feedback from sex steroids and inhibin B.
Klinefelter syndrome is the most common sex-chromosome aneuploidy in males (1 in 500-600 liveborn boys), caused by meiotic non-disjunction of paternal or maternal X chromosomes.

Adolescents develop eunuchoid proportions (tall stature, long legs, span > height by 5 cm), bilateral firm small testes (< 4-6 mL) due to progressive hyalinization of seminiferous tubules, and gynecomastia in 50-80%.

Adults with Klinefelter carry a 20-fold increased risk of male breast cancer, 5-fold risk of metabolic syndrome/type 2 diabetes, extragonadal germ cell tumors (mediastinal teratoma), and mitral valve prolapse.
Testosterone replacement therapy is initiated at age 12-14 years when serum testosterone plateaus and LH/FSH rise, building bone mineral density, lean muscle mass, and preventing metabolic syndrome.

Micro-TESE achieves viable sperm retrieval rates of 40-50% in non-mosaic Klinefelter adolescents and young adults for intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), before complete testicular sclerosis occurs.

Secondary testicular failure can result from bilateral testicular torsion, mumps orchitis, radiation (> 20 Gy to testes destroys Sertoli and Leydig cells), or alkylating chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide > 200-300 mg/kg).

Physiological pubertal gynecomastia affects up to 60% of boys at Tanner stages 2-3, spontaneously regressing in 90% within 1-2 years; refractory severe cases (> 4 cm diameter) respond to tamoxifen or subcutaneous mastectomy.

modules.title: Type 1 Diabetes, Diabetic Ketoacidosis and Neonatal Hypoglycemia

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Type 1 Diabetes: ISPAD 2022 Guidelines, MDI Regimens and CGM Targets

mustKnow.fact: T1D is diagnosed by presence of >= 1 (usually >= 2) pancreatic islet autoantibodies: Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase (GADA), Islet Antigen-2 (IA-2A), Insulin Autoantibodies (IAA), and Zinc Transporter 8 (ZnT8A).

Total daily insulin (TDI) dose is 0.5-0.7 U/kg/day at onset, decreases to < 0.5 U/kg/day during the honeymoon phase (residual beta-cell secretion for 3-12 months), and rises to 1.0-1.5 U/kg/day during pubertal growth spurt.

MDI regimens split TDI into 40-50% basal insulin (long-acting analog: glargine, degludec, or detemir once daily) and 50-60% rapid-acting prandial insulin (aspart, lispro, or glulisine) divided across meals.

International consensus targets: Time in Range (TIR 70-180 mg/dL) > 70%, Time Below Range (< 70 mg/dL) < 4%, Time < 54 mg/dL < 1%, and Glucose Management Indicator (GMI / target HbA1c) < 7.0% (53 mmol/mol).

Carbohydrate coverage is calculated as CIR = 500 / TDI (grams of carbohydrate covered by 1 unit of rapid-acting insulin); Insulin Sensitivity Factor (ISF) for corrections is calculated as 1800 / TDI (mg/dL drop per unit).

Teplizumab (anti-CD3 humanized monoclonal antibody, 14-day IV infusion course) is FDA-approved to delay onset of Stage 3 clinical T1D by a median of 2-3 years in high-risk Stage 2 children (>= 2 autoantibodies with dysglycemia).

Severe hypoglycemia with altered consciousness or seizures requires dry nasal glucagon powder (Baqsimi 3 mg single spray for >= 4 years) or intramuscular glucagon (0.5 mg for < 25 kg, 1.0 mg for >= 25 kg).
Children with T1D require celiac disease screening (anti-tTG IgA) and autoimmune thyroid screening (anti-TPO, anti-TG, TSH) at diagnosis and every 1-2 years thereafter.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Diabetic Ketoacidosis: ISPAD 2022 Protocol, Fluid Resuscitation and Cerebral Edema

mustKnow.term: ISPAD biochemical diagnostic triad for DKA
mustKnow.fact: DKA is defined by hyperglycemia (blood glucose > 200 mg/dL / 11 mmol/L), venous pH < 7.30 or serum bicarbonate < 18 mEq/L, and ketonemia (blood beta-hydroxybutyrate >= 3.0 mmol/L) or moderate/large ketonuria.

mustKnow.term: DKA severity stratification by venous pH
mustKnow.fact: Severity is classified by acidosis: Mild (venous pH 7.20-7.29 or bicarbonate 10-17 mEq/L), Moderate (pH 7.10-7.19 or bicarbonate 5-9 mEq/L), and Severe (venous pH < 7.10 or bicarbonate < 5 mEq/L).

mustKnow.term: Initial fluid bolus volume and timing
mustKnow.fact: Initial fluid resuscitation is 10-20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid (0.9% normal saline or Plasmalyte) infused over 1-2 hours; rapid large boluses (> 20 mL/kg) are strictly avoided to minimize cerebral edema risk.

mustKnow.term: No insulin bolus and delayed infusion start
mustKnow.fact: Insulin is NEVER administered as an intravenous bolus; continuous regular insulin infusion is started at 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr only after 1 hour of fluid therapy has restored intravascular volume.

mustKnow.term: Two-bag system and dextrose addition threshold
mustKnow.fact: When blood glucose drops below 250-300 mg/dL (14-17 mmol/L), 5-10% dextrose must be added to IV fluids (using the two-bag system) to maintain blood glucose between 150-200 mg/dL while continuing insulin to clear ketoacidosis.

Potassium (40 mEq/L as 50% potassium chloride and 50% potassium phosphate) must be added to IV fluids immediately upon establishing urine output and verifying K < 5.5 mEq/L; insulin shifts potassium intracellularly.
Bicarbonate therapy is contraindicated in pediatric DKA because it worsens cerebral intracellular acidosis, causes paradoxical CSF acidosis, hypokalemia, and increases cerebral edema risk.

mustKnow.term: Cerebral edema signs and hyperosmolar therapy
mustKnow.fact: Cerebral edema occurs in 0.5-1% of pediatric DKA, signaled by headache, bradycardia, lethargy, or incontinence; immediately treat with 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg over 15 min) or mannitol (0.5-1.0 g/kg) prior to neuroimaging.

lessonTopics.title: Congenital Hyperinsulinism of Infancy: ABCC8 Genetics, 18F-DOPA and Diazoxide

mustKnow.fact: During spontaneous hypoglycemia (plasma glucose < 50 mg/dL), a critical blood sample confirms hyperinsulinism: detectable serum insulin (> 2-3 microU/mL), suppressed beta-hydroxybutyrate (< 1.8 mmol/L), and absent free fatty acids.

Intramuscular or IV glucagon (1 mg or 0.03 mg/kg) given at the nadir of hypoglycemia triggers an exaggerated glucose rise >= 30 mg/dL within 40 minutes, pathognomonic of inappropriately preserved liver glycogen stores.

mustKnow.term: K_ATP channel molecular genetics (ABCC8 and KCNJ11)
mustKnow.fact: Loss-of-function mutations in ABCC8 (SUR1) and KCNJ11 (Kir6.2) on chromosome 11p15.1 impair K_ATP channel closure, causing continuous beta-cell membrane depolarization and unsuppressed calcium-driven exocytosis of insulin.

Diazoxide (5-15 mg/kg/day divided TID) is the first-line K_ATP channel opener; co-administration with chlorothiazide (7-10 mg/kg/day) is mandatory to prevent fluid retention, pulmonary hypertension, and cardiac failure.

Diffuse hyperinsulinism affects the entire pancreas (autosomal recessive/dominant), while focal hyperinsulinism is caused by a paternal ABCC8 mutation combined with somatic maternal 11p15 loss of heterozygosity in a localized adenomatous cluster.
18F-DOPA PET-CT accurately discriminates focal from diffuse disease with > 95% sensitivity and pinpoints the anatomical location of the focal lesion for curative partial surgical resection.

In diazoxide-unresponsive patients, subcutaneous octreotide (5-30 mcg/kg/day divided QID or continuous SC) inhibits insulin release via somatostatin receptor 5 (SSTR5); monitor for tachyphylaxis and necrotizing enterocolitis in neonates.

mustKnow.term: Subtotal pancreatectomy in refractory diffuse disease
mustKnow.fact: Severe diffuse K_ATP hyperinsulinism refractory to medical therapies requires 95-98% near-total pancreatectomy, carrying a 90% long-term risk of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and exocrine insufficiency.

lessonTopics.title: Monogenic Diabetes: MODY (GCK, HNF1A, HNF4A) and Neonatal Diabetes (KCNJ11/ABCC8)

mustKnow.fact: Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY) is characterized by onset < 25 years, autosomal dominant multi-generational inheritance, absence of islet autoantibodies, preserved endogenous C-peptide, and lack of diabetic ketoacidosis.

Mutations in GCK (glucokinase, 7p13) shift the glucose sensor threshold higher, causing mild, lifelong, non-progressive fasting hyperglycemia (100-145 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.6-7.3%) that does not cause microvascular complications and requires NO pharmacological treatment.

HNF1A mutations cause progressive beta-cell dysfunction, low renal glucose threshold (glycosuria at blood glucose < 180 mg/dL), marked sensitivity to low-dose oral sulfonylureas, and cardiovascular risk.

Mutations in HNF4A cause transient hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and macrosomia (> 4 kg birth weight) in neonates, followed in adolescence by progressive non-ketotic diabetes responsive to sulfonylureas.
Diabetes diagnosed before 6 months of age is monogenic in > 85% of cases and is NOT autoimmune type 1 diabetes; testing for KCNJ11 and ABCC8 mutations is urgently indicated.

mustKnow.term: Oral sulfonylurea transition in KCNJ11 NDM
mustKnow.fact: Over 90% of infants with permanent neonatal diabetes caused by activating KCNJ11 or ABCC8 mutations can be successfully transitioned off insulin injections to high-dose oral sulfonylureas (glibenclamide 0.2-1.0 mg/kg/day).

Severe activating KCNJ11 mutations cause Developmental delay, Epilepsy, and Neonatal Diabetes (DEND syndrome), where high-dose sulfonylureas penetrate the blood-brain barrier and improve neurodevelopment.

Transient NDM resolves spontaneously by 12-18 months of life, caused by overexpression of imprinted genes at 6q24 (paternal uniparental isodisomy or duplication of PLAGL1/HYMAI), though relapsing during puberty.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Type 2 Diabetes: TODAY Trial, Metformin, GLP-1 RAs and Microvascular Screening

mustKnow.term: Aggressive beta-cell failure in pediatric T2D
mustKnow.fact: The TODAY trial demonstrated that beta-cell function declines 3-4 times faster in youth-onset type 2 diabetes (20-35% annual decline) than in adult-onset T2D, leading to rapid oral therapy failure.

Oral metformin is initiated at 500-1000 mg daily and titrated to 2000 mg/day (divided BID) with meals; contraindicated if eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73m² or during acute dehydration/hypoxia due to lactic acidosis risk.

mustKnow.term: GLP-1 receptor agonist approvals in youth
mustKnow.fact: Subcutaneous GLP-1 receptor agonists liraglutide (up to 1.8 mg daily) and once-weekly dulaglutide (0.75-1.5 mg) or semaglutide are FDA-approved in youth >= 10 years, achieving significant HbA1c and BMI reductions.

mustKnow.term: Insulin initiation criteria in new-onset youth
mustKnow.fact: Basal insulin (glargine 0.25-0.5 U/kg/day) must be initiated alongside lifestyle and metformin if HbA1c >= 8.5%, blood glucose >= 250 mg/dL, ketosis, or metabolic decompensation is present at diagnosis.

Unlike type 1 diabetes where screening begins after 5 years, pediatric T2D mandates screening for microalbuminuria (urine ACR >= 30 mcg/mg), diabetic retinopathy (dilated eye exam), and dyslipidemia immediately at diagnosis.

Screening for non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH / MASLD) with serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is mandatory at diagnosis; ALT > 2x upper normal limit persistent for 6 months warrants pediatric GI evaluation.

mustKnow.term: Hypertension screening and ACE inhibitor therapy
mustKnow.fact: Blood pressure >= 95th percentile or >= 130/80 mmHg in pediatric T2D is treated promptly with an ACE inhibitor (enalapril) or ARB, monitoring for hyperkalemia and teratogenicity counseling in adolescent females.

mustKnow.term: Bariatric metabolic surgery criteria in adolescents
mustKnow.fact: Metabolic bariatric surgery (vertical sleeve gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y) is indicated in adolescents with BMI >= 35 kg/m² with severe comorbidities (poorly controlled T2D, severe sleep apnea) or BMI >= 40 kg/m².

modules.title: Rickets, Calcium Disorders and Posterior Pituitary

lessonTopics.title: Nutritional vs X-Linked Hypophosphatemic Rickets: PHEX, FGF-23 and Burosumab

mustKnow.fact: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets manifests with low or normal serum calcium, low serum phosphate, markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase (> 500-1000 IU/L), elevated PTH, and serum 25(OH)D < 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L).

Treatment of nutritional rickets is oral cholecalciferol (vitamin D3 2000 IU/day for 12 weeks, or single-day stoss therapy 300,000-600,000 IU) along with elemental calcium supplementation (500 mg/day) to prevent hungry bone hypocalcemia.
XLH is an X-linked dominant mutation in the PHEX gene (Xp22.1) causing loss of PHEX cleavage and pathological elevation of circulating Fibroblast Growth Factor 23 (FGF-23).

FGF-23 downregulates apical sodium-phosphate cotransporters (NaPi-IIa / NaPi-IIc) in the proximal tubule, causing massive renal phosphate wasting with subnormal TmP/GFR and inappropriately normal/low 1,25(OH)2D.

Burosumab (human anti-FGF23 IgG1 monoclonal antibody, 0.8 mg/kg SC every 2 weeks) normalizes renal phosphate reabsorption, heals rachitic bone lesions, and straightens lower extremity deformities superior to conventional therapy.

Conventional therapy requires oral phosphate solutions (40-60 mg/kg/day divided 4-6 times daily) plus calcitriol (20-30 ng/kg/day); carries high risk of secondary/tertiary hyperparathyroidism and medullary nephrocalcinosis.
Wrist and knee radiographs demonstrate cupping, fraying (brush-like appearance), widening, and splaying of the metaphysis with increased width of the radiolucent physis (growth plate).
Patients with XLH develop recurrent spontaneous periapical dental abscesses in non-carious teeth due to impaired dentin mineralization and enlarged pulp chambers, requiring proactive dental sealants.

lessonTopics.title: Vitamin D-Dependent Rickets Types 1 and 2: CYP27B1, VDR Mutations and Alopecia

mustKnow.fact: VDDR1A is an autosomal recessive deficiency of renal 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1 on 12q14.1), presenting in the first year of life with severe hypocalcemic tetany, rickets, and normal 25(OH)D but undetectable 1,25(OH)2D.
VDDR1A responds dramatically and completely to physiological doses of oral calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3, 0.25-1.0 mcg/day or 20-50 ng/kg/day), bypassing the enzymatic blockade.

VDDR1B is caused by homozygous mutations in hepatic 25-hydroxylase (CYP2R1 on 11p15.2), characterized by low serum 25(OH)D despite high sunlight/vitamin D exposure, responsive to oral calcifediol or calcitriol.

mustKnow.term: VDDR Type 2A vitamin D receptor mutations
mustKnow.fact: VDDR2A (hereditary 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D resistant rickets) is caused by end-organ resistance due to mutations in the vitamin D receptor (VDR on 12q13.11), featuring massively elevated serum 1,25(OH)2D (> 150-300 pg/mL).

mustKnow.term: Total alopecia hallmark in severe VDR defects
mustKnow.fact: Total alopecia (alopecia universalis / absence of scalp hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes) occurs in severe VDDR2A mutants with defective DNA-binding domain, because liganded VDR is required for uncoupled hair follicle cycling.

mustKnow.term: High-dose intravenous calcium rescue in VDDR2A
mustKnow.fact: Patients with alopecia and severe receptor mutations fail massive oral calcitriol doses; healing of rickets requires long-term continuous central venous intravenous calcium infusions (1000 mg/m²/day elemental calcium).
VDDR2B is caused by overexpression of a dominant-negative ribonuclear protein that binds the vitamin D response element (VDRE), preventing VDR interaction, presenting without alopecia.

VDDR3 is caused by a heterozygous gain-of-function recurrent mutation in CYP3A4, which rapidly catabolizes 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D into inactive biliary metabolites, requiring high-dose vitamin D3 to overcome degradation.

lessonTopics.title: Hypoparathyroidism and Pseudohypoparathyroidism: Albright Osteodystrophy, GNAS and PTH Resistance

mustKnow.fact: True hypoparathyroidism features hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and inappropriately low or undetectable serum intact PTH in the presence of normal renal function.

Congenital hypoparathyroidism occurs in up to 60% of infants with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge) due to defective 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouch embryogenesis, accompanied by conotruncal cardiac defects and thymic hypoplasia.

mustKnow.term: Chvostek and Trousseau signs of tetany
mustKnow.fact: Latent hypocalcemia is elicited by Chvostek sign (facial nerve tapping producing ipsilateral facial muscle twitch) and Trousseau sign (carpopedal spasm induced by inflating BP cuff 20 mmHg above systolic for 3 minutes).

Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia (seizures, laryngospasm) requires immediate IV 10% calcium gluconate (1-2 mL/kg or 100-200 mg/kg, max 10 mL) infused slowly over 10 minutes under continuous ECG monitoring.
PHP-1a features target-organ resistance to PTH: hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia with markedly elevated PTH, caused by maternally inherited heterozygous loss-of-function GNAS mutations.

AHO somatic phenotype consists of short stature, rounded moon facies, obesity, subcutaneous ossifications, and characteristic shortening of the 4th and 5th metacarpals/metatarsals (brachydactyly type E).

Paternally inherited GNAS mutations cause PPHP: patients inherit the identical AHO physical phenotype (brachydactyly, short stature) but maintain completely normal serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH due to tissue-specific maternal imprinting.

Maintenance therapy uses oral active vitamin D (calcitriol 20-40 ng/kg/day) and elemental calcium (30-50 mg/kg/day), maintaining serum calcium in low-normal range (8.5-9.0 mg/dL) to prevent hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Central Diabetes Insipidus: Water Deprivation, Desmopressin and Etiologies

mustKnow.term: Classic clinical polyuria threshold in children
mustKnow.fact: Pathological polyuria in children is defined as urine output > 2 L/m²/day (> 4-5 mL/kg/hr in infants), accompanied by persistent intense polydipsia and craving for ice-cold water.
Pediatric central DI is caused by craniopharyngioma / germinoma (30-40%), Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH, 15-20%), neurosurgical trauma, septo-optic dysplasia, or hereditary AVP mutations.

In children presenting with isolated central DI, pituitary MRI reveals thickening of the pituitary stalk (> 3 mm) and loss of the posterior pituitary T1 hyperintense bright spot, mandating staging for bone LCH.
Water deprivation is halted when serum sodium reaches > 145 mEq/L or serum osmolality > 300 mOsm/kg, or if body weight drops by 3-5%; central DI fails to concentrate urine above 300 mOsm/kg.

Subcutaneous or intranasal desmopressin (1-2 mcg SC or 10 mcg intranasal) produces a dramatic > 50% increase in urine osmolality with a prompt reduction in urine volume in central DI, but no response in nephrogenic DI.

Maintenance therapy uses oral desmopressin (0.05-0.2 mg TID) or sublingual melt (60-120 mcg TID), carefully titrated to permit a brief breakthrough diuresis once daily to prevent hyponatremic water intoxication.

Damage to hypothalamic osmoreceptors (post-craniopharyngioma resection) destroys the thirst mechanism; requires rigid daily fixed fluid prescription matched to daily morning weight to prevent severe hypernatremia.

Pituitary surgery or head trauma triggers a classic triphasic response: Phase 1 (transient DI for 24-48h), Phase 2 (SIADH with hyponatremia at days 3-7 from dying neuron AVP leak), and Phase 3 (permanent DI after day 8).

lessonTopics.title: Osteogenesis Imperfecta: Type 1 Collagen Mutations, Sillence Types and Bisphosphonates

mustKnow.fact: Over 85-90% of osteogenesis imperfecta is autosomal dominant, caused by mutations in COL1A1 (17q21.33) or COL1A2 (7q21.3) encoding the pro-alpha-1 and pro-alpha-2 chains of type 1 collagen.

Classified into: Type I (mild, non-deforming, blue sclerae, quantitative defect), Type II (perinatal lethal, crumpling long bones, beaded ribs), Type III (progressively deforming, severe short stature), and Type IV (moderate deforming, normal sclerae).
Blue sclerae result from extreme thinning of scleral collagen fibers, permitting the underlying dark pigmented choroid coat to become visually translucent.
Dentinogenesis imperfecta manifests with opalescent, amber or blue-gray teeth with accelerated attrition and pulp canal obliteration on dental panoramic radiography.
Skull radiographs classically demonstrate >= 10 Wormian bones (mosaic islands of accessory suture ossification > 6 x 4 mm) along the lambdoid suture.

Cyclical intravenous pamidronate (1.0 mg/kg/day for 3 consecutive days every 3-4 months, cumulative annual dose 9 mg/kg/year) increases lumbar spine BMD Z-scores, reduces fracture rates, and reshapes collapsed vertebrae.
Intravenous zoledronic acid (0.05 mg/kg IV infused over 30-45 minutes every 6 months) provides equivalent bone remineralization with fewer hospital visits compared to multi-day pamidronate.
Severe OI types III and IV are complicated by platybasia and basilar invagination (odontoid protrusion into foramen magnum), requiring cervical spine CT/MRI screening for brainstem compression.
